newsitem.title: USA: Trauma Records sues Seagram affiliate Interscope.
newsitem.headline: Trauma Records sues Seagram affiliate Interscope.

text.p: Trauma Records said Tuesday it sued Seagram Co. Ltd.'s 50 percent-owned Interscope Records, seeking $100 million in damages for alleged breach of contract and fraud in a deal involving the hit pop band No Doubt.

The lawsuit also accuses Interscope, which is credited with boosting Seagram's Universal Music division, of negligent misrepresentation, termination of an agreement and extortion, said Trauma's lawyer, Skip Miller.
It alleges that Interscope assigned No Doubt's recording contract to Trauma in 1995 when it was a relatively unknown band but then reneged after the group became hugely popular.
Interscope and Trauma have had a distribution pact since 1994. The lawsuit also seeks to terminate that agreement.
An Interscope spokeswoman said the company had just received the lawsuit and had no futher comment. Universal Music officials were unavailable to comment.

Neither Seagram nor No Doubt, which was first signed to Interscope in the early 1990s, are parties to the suit. Trauma said Interscope assigned the No Doubt contract to Trauma in 1995 after the failure of No Doubt's first album.

Trauma said it spent a lot of time promoting and marketing the group's "Tragic Kingdom" album, which became one of the biggest sellers in 1996. It said Interscope then reneged on its agreement, denying it assigned No Doubt to Trauma. Trauma said. The lawsuit notes Interscope previously acknowledged No
Doubt is on Trauma Record's roster and the band is listed as part of Trauma's roster in industry publications.
The lawsuit also asserts that by threatening to use its leverage of marketing budgets and royalty pipeline payments, Interscope is seeking to disrupt and harm Trauma's business.

Interscope is co-owned by Ted Field, an heir to the Marshall Field fortune. Seagram's Universal Music division has moved from one of the industry's weakest labels to one of its strong players since it paid $200 million to buy a 50 percent share of Interscope over the past couple of years.

Miller said Trauma Records has collected some payments related to No Doubt but has been substantially damaged by virtue of Interscope's actions and seeks recovery of additional damages ancticipated in the future.
